title: May My Life and All My Right Hand Owns Ransom Them
intro: Abu Tammam placed these verses by Abu al-Ghul al-Tuhawi near the beginning of his Hamasa. The commentators connect them to al-Waqba, a watering place contested by Mazin and Shayban. The speaker offers his own life for the riders before giving their names any local setting. By the time he identifies the ground they held, he has already told us the terms on which they deal with others.

translation: May my life and all my right hand owns ransom
the horsemen who justified my faith in them.
1.sharh: The past tense carries the force of a wish: he would give his life and possessions in exchange for theirs. They have already lived up to the confidence that makes the offer possible.

translation: Horsemen who never weary of meeting death
when the mill of kicking war begins to turn.
2.sharh: He names the horsemen a second time and puts them between two images. War grinds like a mill and kicks like a she-camel that will not let herself be milked.

translation: They never repay a good turn with a bad one,
3.sharh: Their conduct has a measure. The first half protects the person who has done them a kindness. The second warns anyone who might mistake that loyalty for weakness.

translation: Their courage never wears thin, though
they have felt the heat of war time after time.
4.sharh: Courage is like a garment that should wear out with use. Repeated exposure to the heat of fighting gives the image its force, since in their case the fabric holds.

translation: They defended al-Waqba's pasture with blows
5.sharh: A particular water and its grazing land give the praise a setting. Al-Marzuqi suggests that men whose deaths might otherwise have been far apart in time and place met them on the same ground.

translation: Their blows turned the enemy's thrust aside.
6.sharh: The turning force is the stroke named one verse earlier. Calling retaliation a cure gives the second half its sting, since the remedy bears exactly the name of the complaint.

translation: They never graze the borders of an easy life
when they make camp, nor the meadows of repose.
7.sharh: Grazing and camping bring back the actual pasture the riders defended. Ease now has borders and rest has meadows of its own, country in which these riders never settle.

1.1.4-5.meaning: “My right hand owns”, all the property at the speaker's disposal.

1.2.2.head: صَدَّقَ
1.2.2.meaning: Confirmed what he thought of them by the way they acted.

2.2.3-4.head: رَحى الحَرب
2.2.3-4.meaning: “War's millstone”, fighting that grinds those caught in it.

2.2.5.head: الزَّبون
2.2.5.meaning: A kicker, especially a she-camel that kicks away the hand milking her.

3.1.5.head: سَيء
3.1.5.meaning: With a bad deed. The adjective has a shortened poetic form.

4.2.1.head: صَلِيَ
4.2.1.meaning: Were scorched or exposed to the heat, here of battle.

5.1.3-4.meaning: Al-Waqba, the watering place and its reserved pasture, contested in the account by Mazin and Shayban.

5.2.3-4.head: أَشتات المَنون
5.2.3-4.meaning: “Scattered deaths”, the separate fates brought together by one encounter.

6.1.1.head: نَكَّبَ
6.1.1.meaning: Turned aside, with the preceding blows as the subject.

7.1.3-4.head: أَكناف الهُوَينى
7.1.3-4.meaning: “The borders of ease”, imagined as land where animals graze.

7.2.5.head: الهُدون
7.2.5.meaning: Stillness or a state of peace, related to the word for a truce.
